title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Authentication

hero.subtitle: The challenge-response authentication framework for HTTP

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP provides a general framework for access control and authentication via an extensible set of challenge-response authentication schemes. This document defines the HTTP Authentication framework, including the 401 and 407 status codes and the Authorization and Proxy-Authorization header fields.

This RFC defines the framework, not individual authentication schemes. Specific schemes like Basic (RFC 7617), Digest (RFC 7616), and Bearer (RFC 6750) are defined separately and plug into this framework.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the HTTP authentication framework: a challenge-response model with the 401 and 407 status codes and the Authorization and Proxy-Authorization headers. It does not define individual schemes. Schemes such as Basic, Digest and Bearer are specified elsewhere and plug into this framework.

sections.title: Authentication Framework
sections.content:
HTTP authentication is based on a simple challenge-response model. The server challenges the client with a 401 (Unauthorized) response, and the client retries with credentials in the Authorization header.

Challenge
The server issues a challenge via the WWW-Authenticate header, specifying one or more authentication schemes it supports.
Credentials
The client sends credentials via the Authorization header. The format depends on the authentication scheme (Basic, Bearer, Digest, etc.).
Realm
The realm parameter defines a protection space. Different realms on the same server may require different credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The server challenges a client with a 401 (Unauthorized) response and a WWW-Authenticate header naming the schemes it accepts. The client retries with credentials in the Authorization header. A realm parameter names a protection space, and different realms on one server can require different credentials.

sections.title: 401 and 407 Responses
sections.content:
Two status codes drive the authentication mechanism, one for origin servers and one for proxies.

Status
Challenge Header
Credentials Header
401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate
Authorization
407 Proxy Authentication Required
Proxy-Authenticate
Proxy-Authorization

A 401 response MUST include a WWW-Authenticate header containing at least one challenge. Without this header, the client cannot determine which authentication scheme to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Two status codes drive authentication. A 401 response comes from the origin server, which is the site itself, and uses WWW-Authenticate and Authorization. A 407 response comes from a proxy and uses Proxy-Authenticate and Proxy-Authorization. A 401 must include at least one challenge.

sections.title: Authorization Header
sections.content:
The Authorization header field allows a client to authenticate itself with an origin server. Its value consists of the authentication scheme followed by scheme-specific credentials.

Authorization Header Examples
Basic authentication (base64 encoded user:password):
Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA==

Bearer token (OAuth 2.0):
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...

Digest authentication:
Authorization: Digest username="user",
realm="example.com",
nonce="dcd98b...",
response="6629fae..."

Basic authentication transmits credentials in base64, which is trivially decoded, so it should only be used over HTTPS. Bearer tokens must also be protected in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The Authorization header holds the name of the authentication scheme followed by scheme-specific credentials, such as Basic, Bearer or Digest. Basic sends the password only base64-encoded, which is trivially decoded, so use it only over HTTPS. Bearer tokens also need protection in transit.

sections.title: WWW-Authenticate Header
sections.content:
The WWW-Authenticate header field indicates the authentication scheme(s) and parameters applicable to the target resource. A server MAY include multiple challenges.

WWW-Authenticate Examples
Single scheme:
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Simple API"

Multiple schemes:
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api",
error="invalid_token"
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="api"

Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos):
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate
Scheme Selection
When multiple schemes are offered, the client should choose the most secure scheme it supports.
Protection Spaces
The realm parameter defines a protection space on the server. The client can reuse credentials for the same realm without waiting for another challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: The WWW-Authenticate header lists the schemes and parameters that apply to the requested resource. A server may offer several, and the client should pick the most secure one it supports. The realm parameter defines a protection space, so the client can reuse credentials there without a new challenge.

subtitle: The challenge-response authentication framework for HTTP

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP authentication lets a server answer a request with a 401 or 407 challenge. The client then retries with credentials in a header. The framework is the same whatever authentication scheme is used.

questions: what is the difference between 401 and 407
what is a realm in http authentication

tldr.problem: Web servers need a common way to ask clients to prove who they are, whatever method of proof is used.
tldr.mechanism: The server replies 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and the client retries with an Authorization header carrying credentials for the chosen scheme.
tldr.outcome: A single framework lets Basic, Digest, Bearer and other schemes plug in; proxies get the same pattern with 407.

today: This framework is still how HTTP authentication works, now restated in RFC 9110. Every API that returns 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header, every browser login prompt for Basic authentication, and every Authorization: Bearer request follows it.

items.title: Credentials

items.text: Names a protection space; different realms may need different credentials.

items.title: Extensible
items.text: New schemes register with IANA and plug into the same headers.
